name: Sugaring paste

card.summary: Sugar-lemon paste that pulls hair out like wax; popular as a gentler alternative, with no head-to-head trials.
card.note: Some products sold as sugar wax contain wax; claims vs waxing are untested.

quick.overview:
Sugaring paste is a sugar-based substance spread on skin and pulled off to remove hair at the root. Fans prefer it to wax because it is water-soluble and can be used at lower temperatures.

It is a temporary method like other epilation. Claims of less pain and fewer broken hairs are widespread but have not been tested in published comparisons.
quick.mechanism: The paste adheres to hair and is flicked or stripped off, pulling hairs out with their roots.
quick.risks: Skin irritation is possible, especially on sensitive skin. Reviews note limited evidence on risks and that studies mostly cover dark hair and fair skin.

lead: Sugaring paste is a sticky mixture, traditionally of sugar, water and lemon juice, spread on the skin and pulled off to remove hair at the root. People use it to get smooth skin on the legs, underarms, face, bikini area and other places, with results that last for weeks, and it is marketed as an alternative to wax.[2][4] Medical literature classes sugaring as a form of epilation alongside plucking, threading, waxing, lasers and electrolysis.[1]

Proponents say the paste grips hair rather than skin, can be used at room temperature or lightly warmed, rinses off with water, and allows another session after about 8 to 10 days of regrowth.[2] The Cleveland Clinic describes the paste as pulled in the direction of hair growth, which it says may break fewer hairs and irritate less than wax, and notes that smoothness typically lasts around three weeks.[4]
Sugaring is also reported as one of the methods used for pubic hair removal.[3] Published research on hair removal covers the category in general; no trials specifically compare sugaring with waxing.

chain: Paste is pressed onto hair-bearing skin
Hair is pulled out with the root
Smooth skin for around two to three weeks
angle.text: Sugaring removes hair from the root, leaving skin smooth without the stubble of shaving. People use it on the face, body and bikini line, and some report softer, finer regrowth after repeated sessions.

infobox: Sugar, water, lemon juice; sometimes honey, cornstarch [2]
Hair ready again after 8 to 10 days [2]; smoothness about three weeks [4]

paras: Home recipes typically combine sugar, water and lemon juice, with cornstarch, honey or molasses in some versions; the acid in the lemon breaks sucrose down into fructose and glucose, yielding a smooth non-crystalline paste.[2] Commercial pastes may add guar gum or essential oils, and some products sold as sugar waxes contain actual wax.[2] The Cleveland Clinic notes that kits are sold for home use while advising against homemade recipes.[4]

In the strip method, the skin is dusted with powder, paste is spread on in the direction of hair growth, and a cloth or paper strip is pressed in and pulled off. In the traditional hand method, a ball of paste is applied against hair growth and flicked off along it, without strips, and residue is rinsed away with water.[2] Hair needs to be at least a few millimeters long for either sugaring or waxing, and sugaring often takes several passes over the same area.[4]

Wikipedia states the method dates to about 1900 BC and was long confined to the region around Persia until the first millennium AD, with honey possibly the earliest sugaring agent. It is known by regional names including sukkar or halawa in the Middle East, agda in Turkey and moum in Iran.[2]

Proponents report less pain than waxing, easier cleanup, lower burn risk because the paste can be used at room temperature, and a shorter wait between sessions.[2] The Cleveland Clinic lists less skin irritation, easy cleanup and possibly softer, thinner regrowth with repeated treatments, and notes that pain tolerance varies.[4] A dermatologist quoted by Cleveland Clinic said every method has pros and cons depending on the person, area, skin type and budget.[4]

A literature review found that most studies of hair removal methods are restricted to darker hair and fairer skin and that all methods besides electrolysis are temporary, each with its own advantages and adverse events.[1]

Irritation or allergic reaction can occur on sensitive skin.[2] Cleveland Clinic lists irritation, inflammation, ingrown hairs (more likely with coarse, curly hair and in skin folds) and sore spots from skin-cell removal as possible effects, and says people who have taken isotretinoin should wait at least six months, and that sunburned, inflamed or infected skin and irritating topicals such as tretinoin are reasons to hold off.[4] A dermatological review of genital hair removal found little evidence on risks for methods such as sugaring.[3]
No studies found specific to sugaring paste. Broader reviews of hair removal practices list sugaring among epilation methods without separate efficacy data.[1][3]
